title: Spaghetti Bolognese
subtitle: Slow-cooked meat ragù with pasta
excerpt: The Emilian ragù that the world calls bolognese: a slow-braised mixture of beef and pork mince cooked down with onion, carrot, celery, white wine, tomato, and milk until it becomes a dense, meaty, deeply flavoured sauce. The process takes hours; the result is worth every minute.

recipe.sourceNotes: Ragù alla bolognese originates from Bologna in Emilia-Romagna and is one of Italy's most codified sauces: the recipe registered with the Bologna Chamber of Commerce in 1982 specifies beef, pancetta, onion, carrot, celery, tomato paste, dry white wine, whole milk, and no garlic or herbs beyond bay. The version spread internationally as spaghetti bolognese, though in Bologna tagliatelle is the traditional pairing (the Bologna food association insists spaghetti bolognese does not exist). The critical technique is the long, slow simmer: the sauce must cook for at least two hours, preferably three, until the liquid has almost entirely evaporated and the fat has separated and re-absorbed into the meat. Adding milk towards the end mellows the acidity and gives the sauce its characteristic richness.

content.text: The time is not optional. At one hour the sauce is good; at three it is transformative. Keep the heat at the lowest possible simmer; if the pot sputters and spits, it is too hot. The fat will separate visibly during cooking and then re-absorb; this is the process working correctly. Use a heavy-based pot with a lid set slightly ajar.

items.preparation: half a tin; crushed by hand

content.text: Melt the butter in a large, heavy pot over medium heat. Cook the pancetta until it has rendered its fat and is golden, about 3 minutes. Add the onion, carrot, and celery. Cook gently for 10 minutes until very soft and sweet, not coloured.

Increase the heat. Add the beef and pork mince. Break up any lumps with a wooden spoon. Cook, stirring, until every trace of pink has gone and the meat is beginning to colour. Pour in the wine. Stir and cook until the wine has fully evaporated, about 5 minutes.

Add the tomato puree and cook for 2 minutes. Add the crushed tomatoes and stock. Stir well. Bring to a bare simmer. Set the lid ajar. Cook for at least 2 hours, ideally 3, stirring every 20 minutes. Add a splash of water if the pot dries out. Thirty minutes before serving, stir in the milk.
Cook the pasta in well-salted boiling water until al dente. Reserve a ladleful of pasta water. Drain the pasta and add to the ragù with a splash of pasta water. Toss to coat. Serve with parmesan.
